about.title: San Juan Bautista Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: San Juan Bautista is a town of about 1,961 people in San Benito County, and most of its storefronts, restaurants, and rentals sit along a handful of streets near The Alameda and Route 156. When a property here is kept up, falls are rare. When it isn't — a wet tile floor with no sign, a broken step at a rental, a parking lot pothole left unpatched — the person who gets hurt often ends up carrying the cost alone. California premises liability law can shift that cost back to the owner, but only if you can show the owner knew about the hazard, or reasonably should have, and did nothing to fix it or warn you. That word, notice, decides most of these cases. Photos of the hazard, the names of anyone who saw you fall, and a prompt written request that the business preserve its camera footage matter more than people expect. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect you with an independent attorney who takes premises cases on contingency, so there is no fee unless you recover.

whyChoose.title: Why San Juan Bautista Residents Use LawProactive After a Fall

items.title: Notice is the whole case
items.desc: California requires proof the owner knew or should have known about the hazard and failed to act. Attorneys in our network know how to dig for inspection logs, prior complaints, and maintenance records that show what the owner actually knew.

items.title: Video disappears fast
items.desc: Many stores overwrite surveillance footage within days. Getting an attorney involved early means a preservation letter goes out before the recording of your fall is gone.

items.title: Deadlines and fault rules that trip people up
items.desc: You generally have two years to file in California, but far less time if the property belongs to a public entity. Under pure comparative fault, being partly to blame reduces your recovery rather than ending it, and an attorney can push back when an owner overstates your share.

items.question: I fell on a cracked public sidewalk near The Alameda in San Juan Bautista. Is the deadline still two years?
items.answer: Probably not. When the property belongs to a city, county, or other public entity, California requires a government claim first, and that claim is generally due within six months of the injury. Missing that window can end the case before it starts, so it's worth speaking with an attorney quickly to confirm who owns the sidewalk and what deadline applies.

items.question: The store says I wasn't watching where I was going. Does that end my claim?
items.answer: No. California follows pure comparative fault, which means your compensation is reduced by whatever percentage of blame is assigned to you, but you aren't barred from recovering. An attorney can challenge a store's version of events with photos, witness accounts, and any footage that still exists.

items.question: It happened at a small, family-run business with maybe one camera. What should I do?
items.answer: Ask, in writing, that they keep any footage from the day you fell, and note the date and time you asked. Photograph the hazard before it gets cleaned up or repaired, and write down what staff said to you at the scene. Small businesses in San Juan Bautista often carry liability insurance, and an attorney can handle the insurer so you don't have to negotiate with a neighbor directly.
